head: They traded tulips
that didn’t exist yet.
slides.sub: The 1637 bubble, and the myth that outgrew it.

image.label: A single streaked tulip on a dark wooden table
image.brief: 17세기 네덜란드 정물화 느낌. 어두운 나무 탁자 위 붉은색과 흰색 줄무늬 튤립 한 송이, 옆에 깃펜과 계약서 종이. 촛불 조명.

head: A flower nobody
could copy on purpose.
body: In the 1630s, the Dutch Republic was rich from trade. Tulips, still new to Europe, became a status symbol for wealthy collectors.
The most prized had flame-like streaks on their petals. No grower could produce them at will. Centuries later, scientists traced the streaks to a virus.

image.label: A Dutch garden of tulips beside a canal house
image.brief: 17세기 네덜란드 운하 주택 옆 정원에 핀 줄무늬 튤립들. 황금시대 분위기, 부드러운 햇빛. 실존 인물 없음.

head: Selling bulbs
still in the ground.
body: Bulbs sit underground most of the year, so traders bought and sold promises: contracts for bulbs to be lifted in summer. Many deals were struck in taverns.
The Dutch called it windhandel, the wind trade. Over the winter of 1636–37, even ordinary bulbs climbed fast.

image.label: Men making deals around a tavern table
image.brief: 1630년대 네덜란드 선술집. 촛불 아래 탁자에 둘러앉은 상인들의 실루엣, 종이 계약서와 맥주잔. 얼굴은 어둡게 처리.

slides.label: guilders, roughly, raised at one bulb auction in Alkmaar in February 1637
body: The bulbs came from the collection of a late tavern keeper and were sold for his orphaned children. Some single bulbs reportedly fetched thousands of guilders, many times a skilled craftsman’s yearly pay.

image.label: A crowded 17th-century auction room
image.brief: 17세기 네덜란드 경매장. 손을 든 군중의 뒷모습, 탁자 위 구근이 담긴 작은 상자들. 따뜻한 갈색 톤.

head: Prices are still climbing.
What do you do?
body: It’s early February 1637. You hold contracts for bulbs you’ve never seen, bought at winter prices, due in summer.

options.text: Buy more contracts while prices keep rising
options.feedback: Everyone around you is making money this way. But each new contract is another promise you must pay in full. Keep swiping.

options.text: Sell your contracts now, even below the latest price
options.feedback: You give up some gains and may look foolish if prices rise. You also need a buyer willing to take them. Keep swiping.

options.text: Hold and wait for summer delivery
options.feedback: Waiting avoids a hasty sale. It also means your fortune depends on strangers honoring their deals months from now. Keep swiping.

image.label: A hand holding a paper contract near a window
image.brief: 창가에서 종이 계약서를 든 손. 창밖은 겨울 네덜란드 거리. 긴장감 있는 차가운 빛.

head: Then, in early February,
the buyers vanished.
body: Days after Alkmaar, buyers at a sale in Haarlem reportedly stopped showing up. Within weeks, trading froze across towns.
Many buyers refused to pay prices they had agreed to in winter. Sellers were left holding promises worth far less than the paper said.

image.label: An empty tavern with scattered papers
image.brief: 텅 빈 선술집, 탁자 위에 흩어진 계약서 종이들. 꺼져 가는 촛불. 쓸쓸한 분위기.

slides.label: of the agreed price Haarlem buyers could pay in 1638 to cancel their contracts
body: Courts were reluctant to enforce deals that looked like gambling debts. Towns pushed for settlements instead, and most disputes ended in compromise.

image.label: Officials at a long table with ledgers
image.brief: 17세기 시청 회의실. 긴 탁자에 장부를 펼친 관리들의 실루엣. 얼굴은 보이지 않게.

head: The legend grew bigger
than the crash.
body: Later retellings, like Charles Mackay’s 1841 book, described a ruined nation. Historians who studied the archives, including Anne Goldgar, found a narrower story.
Losses hit a small circle of merchants and craftsmen. Clear bankruptcies were few, and the Dutch economy kept growing.

image.label: An old book open beside archive papers
image.brief: 오래된 책과 누렇게 바랜 기록 문서가 나란히 놓인 책상. 돋보기 하나. 차분한 도서관 조명.

head: A price that rose
because it was rising.
body: Most buyers weren’t planning to plant anything. They bought because prices were going up, and each higher sale pulled in new buyers.
The whole trade rested on promises. Once some buyers walked away, every contract looked weak, and the loop ran backwards.

image.label: A circular arrow drawn around a tulip bulb
image.brief: 튤립 구근 하나를 둘러싼 원형 화살표 그래픽. 위로 올라가다 아래로 꺾이는 선.

head: Ask what a promise
is really worth.
body: Rising prices can hide that nobody plans to use what they’re buying. A deal is only as solid as the other side’s ability and willingness to pay.
**Try it today:** pick your biggest unpaid invoice or pending deal. What happens if the other side simply doesn’t pay?

image.label: A tulip bulb resting on a signed paper
image.brief: 서명된 낡은 종이 위에 놓인 튤립 구근 하나. 어두운 배경, 은은한 조명.

factChecks.note: 제안된 각도(튤립 계약 가격 폭등과 폭락) 자체는 사실이지만, 네덜란드 경제를 무너뜨렸다는 통설은 과장입니다. Anne Goldgar(2007)의 문서 연구를 따라 피해 범위가 좁았다는 점을 함께 적었습니다.

1637년 2월 알크마르 경매 총액 "약 9만 길더"와 매물이 고(故) 여관 주인 Wouter Winckel의 수집품으로 고아가 된 자녀들을 위해 팔렸다는 점은 Goldgar(2007), Garber(2000) 기준입니다. 경매 날짜(2월 5일 무렵)와 금액을 확인하세요. → [2026-11-02 확인] 1637년 2월 5일 알크마르, 여관 주인 Wouter Winckel 자녀를 위한 경매, 약 9만 길더 확인. 단, 총액은 팸플릿 한 건에 근거한다는 지적이 있어 'roughly' 유지.
"일부 구근이 수천 길더에 팔렸고 숙련 장인 연봉의 몇 배"라는 표현은 정성적으로만 썼습니다. 장인 연봉(대략 수백 길더) 비교는 자료마다 달라 구체 숫자는 넣지 않았습니다.
2월 초 하를럼에서 구매자가 나타나지 않으며 거래가 멈췄다는 이야기는 널리 전해지는 서술이라 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다.
1638년 하를럼 시 당국이 계약가의 3.5%를 내면 계약을 해지할 수 있게 한 결정은 Goldgar(2007) 기준입니다. 비율과 연도를 원문으로 확인하세요. → [2026-11-02 확인] 1638년 하를럼 3.5% 해지 조건은 이번 검색에서 미확인.
줄무늬("broken") 튤립이 바이러스(튤립 모자이크 바이러스, 진딧물 매개) 때문이라는 점은 20세기에 밝혀진 사실입니다.
"windhandel(바람 거래)" 용어와 선술집 모임(colleges)에서의 거래는 Goldgar, Garber 등에서 확인되는 내용입니다. 파산자가 적었다는 서술은 Goldgar의 결론을 풀어 쓴 것입니다.

sources.text: Goldgar, A. (2007). Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age. University of Chicago Press.
Garber, P. M. (2000). Famous First Bubbles: The Fundamentals of Early Manias. MIT Press.
Mackay, C. (1841). Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds.
Trinity College Dublin Library: Tulip mania
